name: T-Deck
tagline: Handheld with keyboard, touchscreen and LoRa. All four bearers; the one you chat from.
summary: LilyGO T-Deck: ESP32-S3 (dual-core 240 MHz, 512 KB RAM, 8 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash), 2.8" 320x240 ST7789 LCD with GT911 touch, QWERTY keyboard on its own ESP32-C3, trackball, microSD, speaker, microphone, USB-C, LiPo connector. Radios: WiFi 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth 5 with extended advertising, and an SX1262 LoRa module (868 MHz on this unit). name: SenseCAP Solar Node P1-Pro
tagline: Solar outdoor LoRa node, nRF52840, no WiFi. LoRa and BLE5 digipeater on a pole.
summary: Seeed SenseCAP Solar Node P1-Pro: nRF52840 (Cortex-M4F 64 MHz, 256 KB RAM, 1 MB flash + 2 MB QSPI) on a XIAO module, SX1262 LoRa (862-930 MHz), L76K GNSS, Bluetooth 5, four 18650 cells, 5 W solar panel, weatherproof case with pole bracket, RP-SMA antenna, USB-C, Grove port. No WiFi, no screen. Runs a port of the XPRS codec and bearer on the Adafruit nRF52 core: beacons, digipeats on LoRa and BLE5, bridges between the two, and dials a T-Deck's GATT channel. Built to sit outdoors unattended.

bluetooth.note: nRF52840 with SoftDevice S140 v7.3.0; one advertising set

bearers.ble5_note: Working, measured 2026-08-30 (docs/ble5-nrf52.md). tinynimble's SoftDevice port speaks to S140 v7.3.0 directly -- Bluefruit, the core's own library, is capped at 31 bytes and cannot carry an XPRS beacon -- and puts a 255-byte extended advert on the air that a T-Dongle digipeated ("via:X3WWAJ"); what it hears on BLE is bridged onto LoRa. The mesh channel over a CONNECTION is measured too (docs/ble5-gatt.md): this board dials a T-Deck serving tn_att, MTU 247, 244-byte frames both ways, hang-up and re-dial. One advertising set on this chip, so the beacon is silent while a session is up.
bearers.lora_note: Working, both directions, measured against a T-Deck on 2026-08-30: 6 of 7 beacons received there at -30 dBm SNR 12, 29 wires received here in 180 s, none corrupt and none unparsed. A beacon from this station was then digipeated by the T-Deck onto the LAN as "via:X3GSLC,X3WWAJ", so the packets are first-class on the network and not merely audible. Driven by RadioLib rather than a port of common/xprs_sx1262, which is ESP-IDF SPI throughout. SF7 / BW125 / CR4-5 / preamble 8 / CRC on, which MUST stay equal to xprslora.c's `xprs` LoRa mode or the two radios are deaf to each other. This board runs the `xprs` mode only: ESP32 stations set to `lora_mode xprs` hear it (verified 2026-09-19, its digipeats arriving as "via:...,X3S7S8"), and ones in the default `meshtastic` mode do not, until it is ported (docs/meshtastic.md, "LoRa modes").
bearers.lan_note: nRF52840 has no WiFi radio, so there is no LAN and there never will be on this board. xprs_bearer_lan is not portable here, and the LAN bearer's task is also what pumps every other bearer's re-air queue -- which is a real structural problem for a port, not just a missing feature. See the note in models/sensecap-p1-pro/README.md.
bearers.espnow_note: ESP-NOW is an Espressif WiFi protocol. No WiFi radio, no ESP-NOW.

xprs.igate_note: No IP on this board, so no APRS-IS.
xprs.api_note: No IP, no HTTP. The station talks only on the air.
xprs.indexer_note: Not ported; the 2 MB QSPI part could hold an archive, nothing writes it yet.
xprs.share_note: Nothing to serve and nothing to serve it over.
xprs.reticulum_note: xprs_bearer_rns is ESP-IDF and TCP; neither exists here.
xprs.ota_note: UF2 over USB only. No signed OTA path on this core yet.
xprs.chat_note: Nothing to type on and nothing to read it from.
xprs.note: A LoRa <-> BLE5 digipeater on a pole. xprs_codec and xprs_bearer verbatim; nothing else of common/.

name: SenseCAP Card Tracker T1000-E
tagline: Credit-card LoRa tracker, nRF52840 + LR1110. A pocket XPRS station: relay, mailbox and position beacon.
summary: Seeed SenseCAP Card Tracker T1000-E: nRF52840 (Cortex-M4F 64 MHz, 256 KB RAM, 1 MB flash), Semtech LR1110 LoRa (863-928 MHz), Airoha AG3335 GNSS, NTC temperature and light sensors, QMA6100P accelerometer, buzzer, one LED and one button, Bluetooth 5, a built-in battery and a magnetic charging cable. No WiFi, no screen. The XPRS station on it is carried by a person: it finds whether Meshtastic or MeshCore is around and lives on that one, repeats the native mesh, carries XPRS between Bluetooth and LoRa, beacons its position (asked of its owner's phone, or its own receiver), temperature and battery, and holds mail for the people it meets.

bluetooth.note: nRF52840 with SoftDevice S140 v7.3.0; one advertising set

bearers.ble5_note: Measured 2026-10-07: hears the bench's stations and the C61 phone, bridges what is worth it onto LoRa, delivers held mail on the bearer the recipient was heard on. The scan listens 10% of the time and rises to 90% for a phone's advertising window, phase-locked to its minute.
bearers.lora_note: Measured 2026-10-07 against a T-Deck in `both` mode: the boot sweep heard its own probe carried back on MeshCore and moved there, and XPRS crosses in both directions in each network's framing. Driven by RadioLib 7.7.1; receive is duty-cycled (preamble sniffing), and the packet length must be re-sent after every transmit (firmware/README.md).
bearers.lan_note: No WiFi radio on the nRF52840, so no LAN.
bearers.espnow_note: ESP-NOW is an Espressif WiFi protocol. No WiFi radio, no ESP-NOW.

xprs.api_note: No IP. It answers q:policy, q:pos, q:temp, q:batt and q:mail on the air.
xprs.indexer_note: It holds mail, not an archive: 64 records in 24 KB of raw flash, class 3 for callsigns whose t:mailbox names it, class 2 for its contacts of the last 30 days. It cannot answer cmd:history and does not announce archive.
xprs.ota_note: The signed GATT update of the P1-Pro (common/xprs_nrf52/update.cpp) is built in; not yet exercised on this card.
xprs.gossip_note: It is gossip's SUBJECT rather than a participant: its signed beacons carry hears: with link:ble, which writes it into the L2 visit history (XPRS.md 12.9.4) of every archiver that hears them.
xprs.chat_note: Nothing to type on and nothing to read it from.
xprs.note: A pocket relay and mailbox. Meshtastic or MeshCore by detection, rechecked hourly.

io.gnss: Airoha AG3335 (GPS / GLONASS / Galileo / BeiDou), UART at 115200

sensors.name: NTC 10K B=4250
sensors.note: the card's own temperature; near body heat in a pocket

firmware.flashing: Serial DFU from the app port (pio run -t upload --upload-port <port>; the 1200-baud touch drops it into the bootloader), or UF2 onto the T1000-E-BOOT volume. The UF2 must be made from the binary at 0x27000: the core's uf2conv.py misplaces an image converted from its hex.

behaviour.title: The first minute
behaviour.text: The LED blinks three times when the radio is up. For about half a minute the card then listens on Meshtastic's LongFast and on MeshCore's default channel, asking each with a small probe that their repeaters carry. It settles on the one that answers (a repeater that carried the probe beats an XPRS station heard, which beats any traffic), remembers it across a restart, and asks again every hour. It only moves to the other network after two hourly checks in a row agree, so one quiet hour does not flip it. With nothing heard anywhere it stays where it was.

behaviour.title: What it carries
behaviour.text: Everything XPRS it hears on LoRa is passed on over Bluetooth. From Bluetooth to LoRa it is choosy, because the channel is shared and every frame costs battery: messages, receipts, reactions, alerts, files, identities and mailbox declarations go out; presence chatter, anything marked scope:local, anything for a person already in Bluetooth range, replays older than half an hour and repeats within half an hour do not. It also repeats the native Meshtastic or MeshCore traffic of the network it is on, the way a stock repeater does, inside the same airtime budget (10% of each hour on the EU 869 MHz band, with a reserve for SOS).

behaviour.title: Where it says it is
behaviour.text: If its owner's phone is within Bluetooth range, the card asks the phone for its position (the XPRS app answers only cards it owns) and uses that, which costs the card almost nothing. Without the phone it switches on its own GPS for one fix, at most every 15 minutes, or every hour when two fixes in a row put it in the same place. It gives up after two minutes indoors. A position older than about 20 minutes is not sent at all.

behaviour.title: What it sends, and how often
behaviour.text: On Bluetooth, every five minutes: position, accuracy, its temperature, battery percentage and voltage, how much mail it holds, and the callsigns it heard directly. On LoRa, every fifteen minutes, a shorter version of the same. Its identity every 30 minutes on Bluetooth and every 3 hours on LoRa, and once an hour a short service line saying it is a portable relay on battery. Everything is signed.

behaviour.title: Your position is public
behaviour.text: The position in these beacons is meant to be heard: anyone on the mesh within range of the card, and anyone the network passes the beacon to, can read where the card is. When your phone answers the card, that is your position. Do not carry the card, or do not make it yours, if that is not what you want.

behaviour.title: It holds mail for the people it meets
behaviour.text: The card keeps up to 64 letters. It holds mail for anyone whose own mailbox declaration names the card, and for people it has met in the last 30 days. When it next hears the recipient directly it hands the letters over on that link, a few at a time, retrying a copy after 30 seconds, 2 minutes and 10 minutes, and forgets a letter once the recipient's signed receipt arrives. Held mail and receipts survive a restart. Because its signed beacons list the devices it heard over Bluetooth, the network learns on its own that this card is the place to route mail for them.

behaviour.title: Making it yours
behaviour.text: There is no claim over the air on this card yet. Connect it by USB and on its serial console (115200, DTR on) type `cfg set own1` followed by your npub, then `cfg set own1c` followed by your callsign; each line saves and restarts the card. From version 1.2.23 the XPRS app notices within a few minutes that the card is yours, starts answering its position questions, and names the card first in your mailbox declaration, so your mail can wait on it.

behaviour.title: Battery
behaviour.text: Built for at least three days on a charge: most of the time the processor sleeps, Bluetooth listens a tenth of the time (more while your phone is advertising), and the LoRa radio only wakes to look for a preamble. The design figure is about 5 mA, roughly five days; it has not been measured over a full discharge yet. A busy mesh to repeat, and using its own GPS instead of your phone, both shorten it.

behaviour.title: Good to know
behaviour.text: The temperature is the card's own, so in a pocket it reads close to body heat. The light sensor and the accelerometer are not used yet. The console prints only with DTR on, and answers one-letter commands (? for its state, S for sensors, w for position, m for mail). To go back to Meshtastic, send D on the console and copy Meshtastic's T1000-E UF2 onto the drive that appears.

name: Video Doorbell WiFi (D340W)
tagline: A doorbell that is its own X4 station: it signs its own ring and airs it on the LAN.
summary: Reolink Video Doorbell WiFi (D340W): a mains-wired doorbell camera on a Novatek NT98566 (ARM Cortex-A9, Linux 4.19.91, read-only UBIFS root), 5 MP OmniVision OS05A10 behind a ~135 degree lens, dual-band Realtek RTL8812CU WiFi, one microSD slot, a LAN port, microphone and speaker. No radio this project's common/ code can drive and not a microcontroller at all: the port is a userland daemon, reobell, a Dart AOT ARMv7 binary baked into a repacked vendor firmware image. It generates a keypair on the camera, derives an X4 callsign from it, announces a signed t:identity every five minutes, and airs signed observations for what the door does: state:pressed on the button, state:motion, state:clear when it goes quiet, each carrying a url: to a still it serves itself on port 8080. It talks on the LAN and does not listen for XPRS, so it is a device on the network rather than a station serving it.

silicon.core: ARM Cortex-A9, ARMv7 EABI5 hard-float (clock not published)

bearers.ble5_note: No Bluetooth radio on this camera; the Realtek part is WiFi only.
bearers.lora_note: No LoRa radio, and no bus brought out to add one.
bearers.lan_note: Transmit only for XPRS, and deliberately so. reobell airs signed wires as UDP broadcasts to port 4242 over the camera's own WiFi association, verified on the bench: real stations on the same LAN reported hearing the camera's derived X4 callsign after its identity and event packets. It opens no XPRS listening socket, so it never repeats what others air and never answers a request. A doorbell that only ever speaks is a smaller thing to leave on a front wall. It does serve plain HTTP on 8080 for the picture its observations point at, which carries no XPRS packet at all.
bearers.espnow_note: ESP-NOW is an Espressif WiFi protocol; this is a Realtek USB part under Linux.

xprs.digipeater_note: Listens to nothing, so there is nothing to repeat.
xprs.bridge_note: One bearer, and it is one-way.
xprs.igate_note: Not ported. The camera has IP, but nothing here speaks APRS-IS.
xprs.hotspot_note: The camera's own AP is the vendor's setup mode, not the XPRS chat hotspot.
xprs.api_note: Not the station API: there is no /api/status and no xprs_api, and common/ is ESP-IDF. What reobell does serve on port 8080 is the camera surface of API-HTTP.md, /door/snapshot.jpg and /door/stream.mjpeg with /api/services beside them, proxied from the camera's own api.cgi so no credential is in a URL it hands out.
xprs.indexer_note: Not ported. The microSD is the camera's recording store.
xprs.share_note: No archive, so nothing to serve.
xprs.ota_note: Firmware arrives as a vendor .pak through the camera's web UI. That path checks a header CRC, the board type and the version, and no signature at all (CVE-2025-60855), which is exactly why this port is possible and exactly why it is not XPRS signed OTA.
xprs.dashboard_note: No screen. The button's LED ring belongs to the vendor firmware.
xprs.note: An X4 device in the sense of spec section 11.7.1, holding its own key instead of a controller holding it for it, and a camera in the sense of 11.7.2: state:pressed, state:motion and state:clear, each with a url: to a still it serves. What is left of 11.7.2 is answering q:snapshot, q:stream and q:state, which needs a listening socket it does not have.

firmware.flashing: The camera's own web UI, System > Maintenance > Firmware Update, with the built .pak renamed to the vendor's filename pattern and a version number higher than the one installed. No signature is checked. The file has to sit somewhere the browser can actually read, which is not /tmp for a snap-confined one. Both qemu validators in tool/ run before any flash.

name: Any ESP32 board
tagline: Try XPRS on the ESP32 board you already have: ESP-NOW, LAN and the walk-up chat hotspot.
summary: For any board built on an original ESP32 with 4 MB of flash or more: the Espressif ESP32-DevKitC, the DOIT DevKit V1, and the many WROOM-32 boards sold under other names (dual-core 240 MHz, 520 KB RAM, WiFi 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth 4.2, USB through a CP210x or CH340). Runs the shared station on ESP-NOW and the LAN, with the HTTP API and the walk-up hotspot whose chat page is how a person uses a board with no screen. It drives no pin, so the one image is safe whatever a board has wired up. No BLE bearer (Bluetooth 4.2 adverts are too short for an XPRS beacon) and no archive (4 MB leaves less room than one index segment).

bluetooth.note: original ESP32: 31-byte legacy advertising only; the firmware leaves Bluetooth off

bearers.ble5_note: Original ESP32, legacy advertising only; an XPRS beacon does not fit. See docs/esp32.md.
bearers.lan_note: Working on the M5Stack Core, the same chip and station; not yet run on a bare devkit.
bearers.espnow_note: Working on the M5Stack Core, the same chip and station; not yet run on a bare devkit.

xprs.hotspot_note: On by default, named XPRS- and the callsign; with no network set, it is how a phone reaches the chat page.
xprs.api_note: Not yet run on a bare devkit.

xprs.ota_note: Two 1.5 MB app slots and the push door.

xprs.note: The M5Stack Core's station without the screen: xprs_app on ESP-NOW and the LAN, headless like the C3.

name: kv4p HT
tagline: ESP32 driving an SA818 VHF transceiver. Packet on 2 m; legacy build.
summary: kv4p HT: an open-hardware VHF handheld interface. ESP32 (dual-core 240 MHz, 520 KB RAM, 4 MB flash) driving an SA818 FM transceiver module (134-174 MHz, 1 W), with PTT, squelch and audio in/out on GPIO, an SMA antenna and a USB-C link to a phone. No screen. Radios: WiFi 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth 4.2, VHF FM. The only board that transmits on an amateur voice band; here it carries packet through xprs_sa818 in the multiboard build.

other.name: SA818
other.note: VHF 134-174 MHz FM module on UART2 (TX 17, RX 16), PTT 18, PD 19, SQ 32, audio out 26 / in 34

bearers.ble5_note: Original ESP32, legacy advertising only; an XPRS beacon does not fit. See docs/esp32.md.
bearers.lan_note: The multiboard build predates xprs_bearer_lan; the chip has WiFi, the code here does not use it as an XPRS bearer.
bearers.espnow_note: Same -- the radio can, the legacy build does not.

xprs.bridge_note: No XPRS bearers in the legacy build.
xprs.igate_note: The legacy APRS-IS iGate (xprs_aprsis) is in main.cpp; not run since the move.
xprs.hotspot_note: Legacy SoftAP with the web chat page; not run since the move.
xprs.api_note: Legacy xprs_http station API; not run since the move.
xprs.ota_note: Legacy xprs_updates path; unsigned, not run since the move.
xprs.mesh_session_note: BLE mesh session is xprs_app / tinynimble; not in the legacy build.
xprs.vhf_note: xprs_sa818 and xprs_radio_tx exist in common/ and the legacy main.cpp drives them; not run since the move.
xprs.note: VHF packet interface. The only board with a transmitter on an amateur voice band.
